questions.q: What does "production-ready" mean for this pipeline, per Fabric & Real-Time Analytics Lesson 43's framing?
options: Surviving the failure modes that eventually show up — malformed events, transient errors, unavailable tables — not just running once successfully
Running without any errors ever occurring in production
Being deployed to a cloud environment regardless of error handling
Passing a single successful end-to-end test run
questions.explain: Lesson 43 defines production-readiness as handling realistic failure modes, which is exactly what this lesson designs for.

questions.q: Why does this pipeline's earlier idempotent MERGE ingestion design (from Lesson 65) directly enable safe retries here?
options: Because a retry after a transient failure produces the same result either way, retrying is safe instead of risking duplicate or corrupted data
Idempotency has no relationship to retry safety
Retries are only safe when using plain INSERT statements, not MERGE
Idempotency only matters for the batch path, not the streaming path
questions.explain: Lesson 11's idempotency principle is what makes "just retry it" a valid recovery strategy rather than a data-corruption risk.

questions.q: What happens to a malformed online-order event in this design, and why does that matter?
options: It's rejected to a dead-letter table by the Eventstream transformation, rather than silently failing or corrupting bronze data
It's silently dropped with no record kept anywhere
It's automatically corrected using AI before landing in bronze
It's allowed into bronze unchanged, exactly like a valid event
questions.explain: Fabric Lesson 35's Eventstream transformations handle this rejection, and dead-letter growth becomes a key metric to watch for schema drift.

questions.q: Why is the alert threshold for the silver-to-gold job set well before the actual SLO breach point?
options: An alert firing only after the SLA is already broken is a postmortem, not an early warning — the threshold gives time to react before the SLO is violated
Alert thresholds and SLOs must always be set to the exact same value
Setting the alert earlier than the SLO has no practical benefit
The SLO itself is irrelevant once alerting is in place
questions.explain: Fabric Lesson 53's alerting and Lesson 56's SLA/SLO framing both point to setting alert thresholds ahead of the SLO so there's time to respond.

questions.q: Which observability signal is described as the metric worth watching most closely in this pipeline, and why?
options: Dead-letter table growth — a slow trickle is normal, but a sudden spike signals an upstream schema change without warning
CPU utilization on the Eventstream compute, which has no connection to data quality
The total number of dashboard page views per day
The color scheme used in the Power BI-style dashboard
questions.explain: A spike in dead-letter growth is exactly the signal Fabric Lesson 51's schema drift and breaking changes lesson warns about.
